question: What must an enterprise SAML IdP support and be configured with to federate into a Cognito user pool?

values.display: supports the [SAML 2.0 standard]
issues JSON web tokens (JWTs)
SP entity ID and assertion consumer service (ACS) URL

evidence.quote: You must choose a SAML IdP which supports the [SAML 2.0 standard](http://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0.html).
With managed login, Amazon Cognito authenticates local and third-party IdP users and issues JSON web tokens (JWTs).
The documentation that follows provides the values that you must provide for the SP entity ID and assertion consumer service (ACS) URL.User pool SAML values quick reference

claim: Sign-in through a third-party IdP is a feature of Cognito user pools and is independent of federation through identity pools, which must be set up separately in each identity pool; a user pool can be a third-party IdP to an identity pool.
question: Is federation in a Cognito user pool the same thing as federation in a Cognito identity pool?

values.display: independent of federation through Amazon Cognito identity pools
A user pool can be a third-party IdP to an identity pool

evidence.quote: Sign-in through a third party (federation) is available in Amazon Cognito user pools. This feature is independent of federation through Amazon Cognito identity pools (federated identities).

Amazon Cognito identity pools, sometimes called Amazon Cognito federated identities, are an implementation of federation that you must set up separately in each identity pool. A user pool can be a third-party IdP to an identity pool.

claim: To an external IdP, Cognito is a service provider: the IdP passes an OIDC ID token or SAML assertion, Cognito maps the claims to a user profile in the user pool, and then acts as an OIDC and OAuth 2.0 IdP to the app, issuing access, ID and refresh tokens; a local user exists only in the user pool directory.
question: What happens inside Cognito when a user signs in through a SAML or OIDC identity provider?

values.display: Amazon Cognito is a service provider (SP)
It generates access tokens, ID tokens, and refresh tokens
A local user exists exclusively in your user pool directory

evidence.quote: To your IdP, Amazon Cognito is a service provider (SP). Your IdPs pass an OIDC ID token or a SAML assertion to Amazon Cognito. Amazon Cognito reads the claims about your user in the token or assertion and maps those claims to a new user profile in your user pool directory.
Amazon Cognito is a combination OIDC and OAuth 2.0 IdP. It generates access tokens, ID tokens, and refresh tokens.
A local user exists exclusively in your user pool directory without federation through an external IdP.

claim: Users can be moved into a user pool in two ways: with a user migration Lambda trigger at first sign-in, where users keep their existing passwords and do not reset them, or in bulk by uploading a CSV file with the user profile attributes.
question: How do the user migration Lambda trigger and CSV import differ for existing passwords?

values.display: There are two ways you can import or migrate users
users can continue using their existing passwords
uploading a CSV file

qualifiers.scope: importing users into a Cognito user pool

evidence.quote: There are two ways you can import or migrate users from your existing user directory or user database into Amazon Cognito user pools. You can migrate users when they sign-in using Amazon Cognito for the first time with a user migration Lambda trigger. With this approach, users can continue using their existing passwords and will not have to reset them after the migration to your user pool. Alternatively, you can migrate users in bulk by uploading a CSV file containing the user profile attributes for all users.

claim: Cognito invokes the migrate user Lambda trigger when a user who does not exist in the user pool signs in with a password or uses the forgot-password flow, and creates the user after the function returns successfully; it is not invoked for passwordless sign-in.
question: When does Cognito call the user migration Lambda trigger?

values.display: doesn't exist in the user pool at sign-in with a password
Amazon Cognito creates the user in the user pool
passwordless sign-in

evidence.quote: When a user doesn't exist in the user pool at sign-in with a password, or in the forgot-password flow, Amazon Cognito invokes this trigger. After the Lambda function returns successfully, Amazon Cognito creates the user in the user pool.

1 Amazon Cognito doesn't invoke this trigger when users authenticate with [passwordless sign-in](amazon-cognito-user-pools-authentication-flow-methods.md#amazon-cognito-user-pools-authentication-flow-methods-passwordless).

claim: User pool Lambda triggers let you add your own authentication challenges, migrate users from another identity store, customize messages and modify JWTs; a trigger can even prevent sign-in by a user who would otherwise succeed.
question: What can Cognito user pool Lambda triggers do?

values.display: introduce your own authentication challenges
modify JSON web tokens (JWTs)
prevent sign-in by a user who would otherwise succeed

evidence.quote: Within the system of request and response events, you can introduce your own authentication challenges, migrate users between your user pool and another identity store, customize messages, and modify JSON web tokens (JWTs).
For example, you can prevent sign-in by a user who would otherwise succeed.

claim: Threat protection (formerly advanced security features) monitors and can automatically shut down malicious activity in a user pool, can run in audit mode that only publishes metrics to CloudWatch, and is available in the Plus feature plan.
question: What is Cognito threat protection, which feature plan includes it, and can it run without blocking?

values.display: available in the Plus feature plan
use audit mode to gather metrics
formerly called *advanced security features*

evidence.quote: Threat protection is available in the Plus feature plan.
Or you can use audit mode to gather metrics on detected risks without applying any security mitigations. In audit mode, threat protection publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch.

Threat protection, formerly called *advanced security features*, is a set of monitoring tools for unwanted activity in your user pool, and configuration tools to automatically shut down potentially malicious activity.

claim: Compromised-credentials detection compares users' credentials with leaked credential lists and common passwords in username-and-password standard authentication flows; it does not detect compromised credentials in SRP or custom authentication. Adaptive authentication reviews location and device information and responds to risk automatically.
question: In which authentication flows does Cognito detect compromised credentials?

values.display: doesn't detect compromised credentials in secure remote password (SRP)
review location and device information

evidence.quote: You can check for compromised credentials in username-and-password standard authentication flows in user pools. Amazon Cognito doesn't detect compromised credentials in secure remote password (SRP) or custom authentication.
Amazon Cognito can review location and device information from your users' sign-in requests and apply an automatic response to secure the user accounts in your user pool against suspicious activity.

claim: Adding a domain gives a user pool managed login: an OAuth 2.0/OIDC authorization server, ready-to-use sign-in, sign-out and password pages, and a service provider to SAML, OIDC and social IdPs; the classic hosted UI is the first-generation alternative, the two are not used together, and in the Lite plan the classic hosted UI is the only option.
question: What is Cognito managed login, and how does it relate to the hosted UI?

values.display: A ready-to-use user interface (UI)
The classic hosted UI is a first-generation version
the classic hosted UI is your only option

evidence.quote: + A ready-to-use user interface (UI) for authentication operations like sign-in, sign-out and password management. The *managed login pages* act as a web front end for authentication services.
You choose one or the other for a user pool domain—managed login and the classic hosted UI aren't used together. The classic hosted UI is a first-generation version of the managed login services.
In the Lite [feature plan](cognito-sign-in-feature-plans.md), the classic hosted UI is your only option for user pool domain services.

claim: Cognito quotas apply per AWS account and Region and are shared by all tenants of an application; the managed login session cookie authenticates local users for all app clients of the same user pool, and per-tenant user pools are one way to prevent sign-in across app clients.
question: What decides between one shared user pool and per-tenant user pools in a multi-tenant app?

values.display: shared across all tenants in your application
for all app clients in the same user pool
Separate your users into per-tenant user pools.

evidence.quote: Amazon Cognito [quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/quotas.html) are applied per AWS account and AWS Region. These quotas are shared across all tenants in your application.
When you authenticate *local users* in a user pool, their session cookie authenticates them for all app clients in the same user pool.
+ Separate your users into per-tenant user pools.
